name: God the Father
role: Ruler of Heaven; foresees the Fall before it happens
description: Category A, dramatized -- with a real theological controversy attached. Milton stages God as a speaking character (principally Book III), itself bolder than anything the Bible does directly. Milton's own private treatise De Doctrina Christiana (unpublished in his lifetime, manuscript discovered 1823/published 1825) argues Father and Son are 'two distinctly separate beings,' the Son subordinate and begotten in time -- a position modern scholars label Arian/subordinationist. Whether the poem's verse itself commits to this heterodoxy (vs. only the prose treatise) is a live, unresolved scholarly debate (Rumrich vs. Lieb). See docs/milton/character-catalog.md §IV and docs/milton/theology-and-sources.md §1.
narrative_function: Heaven's court and the poem's stated antagonist-of-the-thesis: this book's narrative POV frames His court in explicit monarchical/slaveholding imagery, per docs/planning/TFAH-brief.md §8 -- the nonfiction apparatus must not present this framing as literary-critical consensus (Lewis's orthodox defense is a real, serious counter-position).
